entry.evidence: Little is known about groundwater flow patterns and water quality in the shallow aquifer below the peat.

steps.action: Stated two aims: identify groundwater flow patterns and controls of water-table fluctuations, and estimate groundwater discharge from peatland to sea.
steps.quote: [...] of this study were (i) to identify groundwater flow patterns and related controls of water table fluctuations

steps.action: Drilled 16 sediment cores, probed and kriged peat thickness with archival data, and installed 14 groundwater and 3 ditch observation wells with 15-minute pressure, temperature and conductivity loggers, with a head-error budget.
steps.quote: A total of 14 groundwater observation wells were installed at 7 locations (Fig. 1).

steps.action: Estimated hydraulic conductivity from falling- and rising-head slug tests analysed with the KGS model in AQTESOLV.
steps.quote: using the KGS-model (Kansas Geological Survey; Hyder et al., 1994) to obtain radial hydraulic conductivity parameters

steps.action: Sampled groundwater and surface water in August 2017 and April 2018 for major ions, nutrients and carbon, and the lower-sand wells in early 2017 for tritium-helium.
steps.quote: Groundwater samples were obtained from all groundwater wells, except for MP3 due to technical problems, in August 2017 and in April 2018.

steps.action: Defined apparent piston-flow tritium-helium ages, correcting tritiogenic 3He for equilibrium, excess-air (via neon) and radiogenic components.
steps.quote: Apparent piston-flow groundwater ages were determined with the tritium–helium method

steps.action: Converted point-water heads to equivalent freshwater heads after Post et al. (2007) and set up Darcy flow-velocity calculation with measured K and literature porosity.
steps.quote: To consider the influence of density, equivalent freshwater heads

steps.action: Tested a density-corrected horizontal gradient between 7LS and 6LS and found the effect negligible, so dropped it.
steps.quote: This method was tested, but the effect was negligible with less than a centimetre difference

steps.action: Reconstructed the stratigraphy (till, fine sands, gyttja, peat) and interpreted a deep till depression below the beach as an ancient glacial river valley.
steps.quote: We assume that this is part of an ancient glacial river valley

steps.action: Described head time series: a land-to-sea gradient, a near-zero gradient in the central peatland, coastal heads following sea level, and seasonal vertical flow reversals.
steps.quote: A hydraulic gradient from land to sea prevailed.

steps.action: Mapped specific conductivity, chloride, sulphate, nutrients and dissolved carbon along the transect.
steps.quote: The groundwater in the peatland was enriched in nutrients and dissolved carbon.

steps.action: Estimated apparent tritium-helium ages (7 to 56 years, 2LS undatable), tritium-free fractions, ΔNe and radiogenic 4He along the forest-to-coast transect.
steps.quote: ΔNe was 1 % in the forest and decreased to

steps.action: Checked ages with duplicate analyses and with radiogenic 4He as an independent residence-time tracer.
steps.quote: Analytical uncertainties of duplicates of this study were lower than 5 % for tritium

steps.action: Calculated a Darcy lateral travel time of about 7,200 years between 7LS and 6LS from current gradients.
steps.quote: The calculated lateral groundwater travel time based on current hydraulic gradients is approximately 7,200 years between 7LS and 6LS.

steps.action: Compared gradients with ditch layout, ditch depth and peat thickness, inferring that ditches still control flow where they cut into the aquifer.
steps.quote: The ditch system still impacts on groundwater flow in the peatland, despite rewetting.

steps.action: Checked seawater routing through ditches with conductivity after the January 2017 storm surge and a second, later surge.
steps.quote: A similarly short time lag has also been observed for a later storm surge

steps.action: Weighed recharge through peat against an origin in the mineral aquifer using ΔNe and radiogenic 4He, and related age to peat thickness.
steps.quote: supports the assumption that most water originates from recharge through the peat and not from the mineral aquifer

steps.action: Checked downward flow in the peat against soil conductivity profiles at MP6 and pore-water profiles from Koebsch et al. (2019).
steps.quote: The SC distribution further supports this assumption

steps.action: Assembled a conceptual flow-path model: infiltration of ponded surface water, forest groundwater diverted by ditches, and local discharge to ditches or coast.
steps.quote: In summary, we assume that input of water into the peatland is mainly through infiltration of surface water ponding at the surface

steps.action: Used SGD rates calculated by other studies (75-130 l/d per m) to discuss terrestrial SGD and nutrient export.
steps.quote: The average SGD at the study site calculated by different studies yielded values between 75 and 130

steps.action: Estimated seawater fractions from chloride against the Baltic Sea endmember: 24 ± 4 % in peat and 30 ± 3 % in the aquifer.
steps.quote: indicates that 24 ± 4 % (average ± standard deviation of all samples from 2P, 6P, 7P) of the water in the peat

steps.action: Excluded evapotranspirative concentration as the chloride source, citing positive water balance, no long-term SC rise and fresh near-surface pore water.
steps.quote: The increased Cl- concentrations cannot be caused by ET, since the climatic water balance is positive

steps.action: Excluded subsurface saltwater intrusion (except at 1LS) because chloride decreases toward the coast and beach soil SC does not rise with depth.
steps.quote: Subsurface intrusion of saltwater – the other possible pathway – is unlikely

steps.action: Kept past and ditch-borne inundations as the main seawater pathway, with regular past floods implied by homogeneous chloride across ages.
steps.quote: We assume inundations as the main pathway of the seawater into the peatland

steps.action: Compared seasonal flow reversals and SC amplitude by screen depth with inland-peatland studies, concluding reversal intensity decreases with depth.
steps.quote: These observations indicate that the intensity of flow reversals in the peat decreases with depth.

steps.action: Concluded that rewetting mainly affects the upper peat, ditches still set local flow fields, and rewetting may revive SGD, and called the patterns transferable.
steps.quote: Rewetting (and preceding drainage) of coastal fens is concluded to have limited impact on deeper groundwater and to mainly influence the upper peat.

end.claim: Recharge of surface water through the peat is a major groundwater source, ditches still control local flow, and rewetting mainly affects the upper peat with little impact on the underlying aquifer.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the tritium-helium ages, ΔNe and radiogenic 4He along the transect, recharge through the peat and the long system memory could not be inferred from heads alone, which differ within measurement error.

gates.evidence: Wells and sampling followed general aims, not a stated hypothesis (p. 2). Rival chloride sources and pathways were tested against data that could have favoured them (p. 9), but the main flow-pattern claim rests on interpretation, with head differences often within measurement error (p. 8). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

limits: The supplied XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so body steps cite printed pages and their quotes come from the PDF. The supplementary material (S1-S6), cited for logger details, age data, soil SC and storm-surge SC, was not supplied. Aim (ii), estimating discharge to the sea, is not performed here: SGD rates are taken from other studies, including the authors' own thesis and co-authored work (p. 9). Tritium-helium sampling was one campaign at five wells, and 2LS was undatable. The 7,200-year Darcy travel time conflicts with the apparent ages, but the paper does not reconcile the two (inference). The authors state that vertical head differences at MP6 and MP7 are often within measurement accuracy (p. 8). The claim that the flow patterns are transferable to other coastal peatlands is not tested (p. 10). Sub-claims and their statuses: seawater fraction of 24-30 % (estimate_with_resolution); ages of 7 to 56 years (estimate_with_resolution); flow-reversal intensity decreasing with depth (regularity_in_range, one site); seawater entering via inundation rather than subsurface intrusion (best_explanation). Data are available on request only, and no review file was supplied.
